sections.content:
The course is mainly focused on the reformation policies of China during the 80-90s. A lot of historical context regarding the events and turmoil during Mao's reign is covered.

Some of the core ideas discussed:
- Political structure of CCP
- Evolution of the economic system
- Household registration system (戶口制度)
    -> Rural / urban divide and internal migration
- Social organisations
    -> Work units (單位), people's communes (人民公社), etc.
- Social stratification
- Education inequality
- Population control

There are no official prerequisites, but having a basic understanding of China and (perhaps) a bit of knowledge in economics would help.

There are additional readings every week which is part of the exam syllabus, in the form of textbook excerpts and academic papers. I recommend reading the papers (especially those authored by the lecturer) as those are more likely to appear in the exams.
sections.teaching:
The lectures are mostly boring. He seems to be enthusiastic about what he is talking about - partly because most of the lecture contents fall within his field of research. However, he stammers a lot which makes it slightly difficult to pay full attention to what he is talking about. Another problem is that his lectures overrun a lot - sometimes by 20 min or more.

This may seem obvious but expect a lot of unfamiliar Chinese / CCP phrases and slogans in the lecture notes.

TAs are quite helpful and give hints on how to prepare for the exams.
sections.grading:
Grading policy are as follows:
15% Attendance / participation
40% Midterm
45% Final

Both midterm and final are conducted over Zoom this semester. Students can refer to all of the notes, readings and tutorial slides during the exam.

Midterm: Mean 28.7/40, SD 4.23
Final: Mean 34.7/45, SD 5.06

I scored +1.2 SD for midterm, +0.4 SD for final, got A- in the end. Not bad considering that I have no prior knowledge about the topic whatsoever.
sections.workload:
Extremely light workload, at least for this semester. Open-book exams with MC questions only. No homework / projects / quizzes of any sort. This is pretty much the only reason I chose this course to fulfill the SA-SSC requirement.

Attendance will be taken so remember to attend all tutorial sessions.

sections.content: Very satisfying. At least it suits my interest. You should not miss this course if you are interested in this subject.
sections.teaching: Lectures are quite sleepy. Tutorials are interesting and interactive. The PPTs are designed really concise and informational at the same time. The readings are also highly relevant and smartly written. I can see the efforts that the instructor put into this course.
sections.grading: Be careful about MC exams. Errors cost a lot. The two exams are all open-book, but it can be tricky. Not much stress, and especially fun if you take this course with your friend and have someone to discuss class topics with.
sections.workload: I guess about 70% of PPT slides are "informational item" which is not going to appear on the exam. It is a relief, but I do recommend you to have enough background knowledge. Optional reading really helps but there's a lot. You will need a comprehensive understanding, so it is important to listen to lectures and read. No assignment, so this course helps to manage your time in this semester.

sections.grading:
Don't take this course if you are a Hongkonger. Otherwise, you will regret. Why do I say that? Because there are lots of mainlanders who have registered the course. They already understood everything but to compete the good grade with you. The course is originally a good grade course, but only for mainlanders only.

It is very hard to compete with them. The exam is mc, but it is very hard to do to be honest. You can't find the ans in the ppt for some of the questions.

My result is very bad, with midterm lower than 1sd from the mean.

Midterm: 16/25 mean: 19
Final: 28/40 mean: 30

It is a very terrible course. But luckily I can decide Pass or Fail or not.
Grade: Pass
If choose regular grade I will be most likely to get B-.

sections.content: General knowledge about Contemporary China.  The course mainly talks about China development in 1949-2000s in terms of political, economic and social aspects. Those who have taken history as DSE elective would have an advantage.
sections.teaching: Very nice pro and TA. They are always willing to answer questions and reply to emails quickly.
sections.grading:
Competitive
a few scores can make a grade difference

Exams all MC and open notes so many people can get a high score.
sections.workload:
0 workload
Only mid-term, final exam, participation in tutorials and attendance in class and tutorials.
There are reading materials but I never read it. Notes in the lecture are enough.

sections.content:
The content is separated into two parts: the first half and second half. They will be separately tested so you don't have to memorize/study everything taught in the term before one exam (which is rather good for procrastinators).
The content covers reforms of Modern China, and they are not very complicated if you have basic knowledge about Chinese society.
sections.teaching:
The professor's voice is rather boring, I almost slept every class.
The TAs are basically reading aloud their powerpoints, no attendance is taken so you can skip the tutorial class if you don't have specific questions to ask them.
sections.grading:
This course has in-class quizzes randomly so you have to attend every class to make sure you didn't skip a quiz. Overall the answers are easily accessible in powerpoint notes, but sometimes it asks things that the professor talked about in class.

There are a midterm and final exam with MC only, they are open-book so you can bring all your notes with you.
sections.workload:
Almost no workload.
There are no assignments, but 1-3 readings per week. You don't actually have to read them because they are very long and boring. Except that you may have to bring the readings in the exam because quite a few of the questions are related to the content of the readings. (better if you read them once and highlight the mainpoints)

sections.content:
COURSE OUTLINE AND SCHEDULE (Subject to Revision)

Week 1
Course Introduction
The Study of Chinese Society
Reading: 
Stockman Chapter 1 “The Study of Chinese Society” Pp. 1-22
Wu, Xiaogang 2012 “Social Change” in Handbook of Contemporary China, edited by William Tay and Alvin So, World Scientific

Week 2
Historical Briefing: From Revolution to Economic Reform
The Mao Years (Documentary)
Reading: 
Lieberthal Chapters 3 “The Maoist System: Ideas and Governance”; Chapter 4 “The Maoist Era” Pp. 57-121
Naughton Chapter 3 “The Socialist Era, 1949-1978: Big Push Industrialization and Policy Instability” Pp. 55-84. 

Week 3
The Chinese Communist Party and Ideology
Reading: 
Readings:
Stockman Chapter 6. “Power and Revolution: Economic and Political” Pp 120-148. 
Lieberthal Chapters 6. “The Organization of Political Power and Its Consequences: The View from the Outside” & Chapter 7 “The Organization of Political Power and Its Consequences: The View from the Inside” Pp. 155-218.
Tutorial Week (Background and History) (Feb 11 & 14)

Week 4
The Socialist Economy and Economic Reform
Reading: 
Lieberthal Chapter 5 “The Reform Era” Pp. 122-153
Naughton, Chapter 4 “Market Transition: Strategy and Process” Pp. 85-111

Week 5
Open-door Policies and Economic Globalization
Reading: Naughton 2007, Chapter 16-17
Tutorial Week (Chinese Economy) (Feb 25 & 28)
Week 6
The Household Registration (Hukou) and Rural-Urban Migration
Reading: 
Naughton Chapter 5. “The Urban-Rural Divide” Pp 113-135
Kam Wing Chan 2009. “The Chinese Hukou at 50” Eurasian Geography and Economics, 50(2): 197–221 (J).
Week 7
Midterm Exam in Class
Tutorial Week (Mid-term Review) (March 11 & 14)
Week 8
Rural Economy and Society
Reading:
Naughton Chapter 10, “Rural Organization” Pp 229-250
Naughton Chapter 12 “Rural Industrialization: Township and Village Enterprises”, Pp 271-294

Week 9
The Urban Work Unit (Danwei) System and Its Transformation
Reading: 
Bian, Yanjie 1994. Work and Inequality in Urban China, pp. 23-50. Albany, N.Y.: State University of New York Press.
Xie, Yu and Xiaogang Wu. 2008. “Danwei Profitability and Earnings Inequality in Urban China.” China Quarterly 195: 558-81 (J).
Tutorial Week (Hukou and Migration) (March 25 & 28)
Week 10
Changing Employment, Changing Inequality
Reading: 
Friedman, Eli and Ching Kwan Lee. 2010. “Remaking the World of Chinese Labour: A 30-Year Retrospective.” British Journal of Industrial Relations 48(3):507–33 (J).
Wu, Xiaogang 2019. “Inequality and Social Stratification in Post-socialist China." Annual Review of Sociology (J).
Week 11
Access to Educational Opportunities
Reading: 
Wu, Xiaogang and Zhuoni Zhang 2010 “Changes in Educational Inequality in China, 1990-2005.” Research in Sociology of Education, Volume 17, 123–152
Wu, Xiaogang 2017. “Higher Education, Elite Formation and Social Stratification in Contemporary China: Preliminary Findings from the Beijing College Students Panel Survey.” Chinese Journal of Sociology 3(1):3-31 (J)
Tutorial Week (Work Units and Stratification)
Week 12
Population Issues: One Child Policy and Population Aging
Class Wrap up
Reading: 
Wang Feng, Yong Cai, and Baochang Gu 2012. “Population, Policy, and Politics: How will History Judge China’s One-Child Policy?” Population and Development Review 38: 115-129 (J).

Week 13
Tutorial Week (Education, Population, and Final Review) (May 6 & 9)

sections.content: The course illustrates modern China in forms of political and socioeconomic aspects. The course would introduce some background information and then the details of a particular phenomenon in China. I would consider this course as a Chinese history one.
sections.teaching: Prof. Wu usually just recites from the PPTs, but sometimes he would try to interact by asking questions in the classroom and tell some interesting side-track stuff.
sections.grading:
Very good, since I have an interest in Chinese history stuff. The grading policy and exam format are much nicer than before.

For the grading policy, there are no longer projects and presentations. For the exam format, nowadays open-booked is allowed. (My secondary school classmate is so stupid to drop this course due to the fact that the prof.'s teaching is boring... this course is a very good grade one, the prof. just distribute A-range freely.

Class performance (15%): I think this category is dominated by 5 in-class quizzes (attendance), you can get full marks by some sort of "cheating" with the PPT without getting caught by the prof. (I think nearly everyone did this) I got 13/15 for the summation of all quizzes
Midterm (40%): 35/40 (87.5/100, above mean 1 sd)
Final (45%): Unannounced
Overall: A (I think I probably get more than 90% correct in the finals)
sections.workload: No homework and projects, but preparing the open-book materials for the exam do require some effort especially the readings. The prof. said about one-fourth of the content in the exams are from readings. You can still guess most of the reading-related questions if you have some sense to the issues and you are concentrated enough in class.

sections.content: The lecture was basically about China covering the aspects of economic, political, and so on. The content was not very difficult to understand as the instructor processes the lecture with lecture notes. However, paying attention to the instructor is still important.
sections.teaching: His teaching was good. Although sometimes I could not understand him clearly, all of the information given by the instructor in the class was important and helpful.
sections.grading: The grading may be intensive since most of the students achieve very good grade. The exam (in my opinion) was not that difficult, and a lot of students earned very high points in the exam. Therefore, I think concentrating in the class and listening to the instructor is important to earn a high grade in this class.
sections.workload:
I don't think that the workload was that much heavy.
However, it still does not mean that the student cannot spend any time studying the course :)
Some people may think that the content is super easy, but for international students (such as me), I still had to study in order to get a fine grade.

sections.content:
係時候又要想當年黎鼓勵下大家

是咁的

兩年前我就take左SOSC1350，咁呢個course就凈計attendance、midterm同final既者，而midterm同final就全MC，open notes。

咁我midterm都做得唔太好，錯左兩題，無左3.X%course grade。所以我唯有attendance take足再加final爆seed

而到左考final個日，我一起身就特別精神，考試亦做得特別快。兩個鐘既考試，我一個鐘都唔使就做晒40題MC，再加上我之後有試，咁我大概45分鐘就舉手交卷。個TA都嚇親，過黎收卷之餘仲等埋我一齊行出試場。沿路見到一班人R晒頭，仲奮鬥緊，見我提早交卷早走個種眼神，我睇得出愕然同埋羨慕。

唔知大家有無試過提早交卷肯定自己一定滿分，呢種智商上既優越感
真係好爽

咁出到去試場，個TA就問我:做好晒啦?咁早走?

但我無正面回答佢，我只係問佢: 呢個Course攞幾多percent先有A-range

TA: 未知架，要等professor定，你好有信心wo

我: 哦，無啊，問下者，今個sem多謝晒，拜拜

而我最後final 滿分 攞A+

人生試一次呢種經歷真係

sections.content: the course only covers the very basic knowledge of contemporary China. Not difficult to understand. Part of the content is quite similar to HKDSE’s Liberal Studies.
sections.teaching: not bad, but it is a bit boring. You can choose to skip class if you’re already very familiar with the history and development of China. But I recommend those who didn’t study Chinese history in high school to pay attention in class in order to get a good grade.
sections.grading: if you have paid attention in class, both midterm and exam would be easy to score high. No need to worry if you’re not familiar with Chinese history because paying attention in class does help a lot, you could still compete with those who have studied Chinese history before.

sections.content: Compulsory course for GCS year 1 students. It's all about the evolution of China from 1911 to nowadays economically, socially etc. Not necessarily a course for you if you've already had an adequate understanding of Chinese history cuz you already know everything, but if you want to get a good grade then go ahead.
sections.teaching:
Prof. Lin is a passionate teacher, he'll answer any question you have for him in great detail. His teaching is quite boring tho cuz he has that monotone voice, so its easy for you to fall asleep BUT PLEASE DONT cuz a lot of questions in exams are based on his verbal presentation instead of the powerpoint.
You can skip class if you have enough knowledge/common sense to answer the questions in exams, just ask someone to sign for you.
sections.grading:
Really good, if you took Chinese history as an elective in high school/know a lot about contemporary china/have enough common sense then you have no problem getting an A range grade ;)
Picking the right mc answers in exams is a real pain in the ass tho, cuz sometimes all four of them are seemingly correct, so yea, just a heads up. Overall you can slack in this course and still get a really good grade.
And the efficiency of the prof and TAs is impeccable, got the grades a few hours after the final exam :D hate it when the staff move at a glacial pace.
sections.workload: LOL this course seriously requires no workload except taking notes in class. No quiz, no assignment, no discussions, no readings, just go to class and listen to what Prof. Lin has to say. You don't even need to study for exams (open-book :D), just flip through the powerpoints and notes the night before and you're good to go.

sections.content: The content of this course is about the situation of contemporary China（1949-now), which covers different aspects such as politics, economy, social and culture. In this semester there is a total of 7 parts of notes. Mid term will examine the first 3 notes and the rest in final.
sections.teaching: The professor is a good guy but his lectures were extremely boring. He basically speaks in just a single tone and made students extremely hard to maintain focus. The content of his lecture is basically same as the notes, However, additional information which will be useful for the exam will be mentioned during lectures, Students who aim A range should pay attention, or else, you can just skip the lecture and go to tutorials.
sections.grading:
As the mid term and final are both open-book exams which only consists of MC questions, the mark range of this course is extremely tight. Students with prior knowledge/ familiar with modern China history will have advantage.

Also the grading is quite good. :D
sections.workload:
One mid-term and One final and attendance. Nothing else.
Extremely little workload as it is an open book exam.

sections.content: The content is quite overwhelming. If I remember correctly there were 6-7 topics. Most of the are quite large.
sections.teaching: I enjoyed the teaching but you had you go to every class in order to jot down everything the professor says because he will not be testing on what the power points already give you. He will be mentioning key points during the lectures that you have to write down and remember for the midterm and final
sections.grading: Grading is the same for everyone. Multiple choice questions. Though, for a history exam, I would much prefer to write essays.. I do not understand why a history examination requires multiple choice answers. Also the multiple choice answers are quite difficult as none of the answers are totally wrong. He likes to put all correct answers but for you to pick out the best answer for the question, which is super annoying.

sections.content: Introductory course about Chinese development in the pre and especially post-Mao era. The professor includes both qualitative and quantitative economic and sociological data on slides, and assesses the historical progression of China through social, political, economic lenses.
sections.teaching: Teaching is lecture-based, with one lecture per week, and tutorials every two weeks. Tutorials revolve around discussion of a video clip that is around 60 minutes. The instructor has good english and likes to deviate from what is seen on the slides, he does not read off the slides. Attendance is important in order to gain additional information and analysis of slide content before the exam.
sections.grading: All-multiple choice and open-book midterm and final. Participation grades are not difficult to get in tutorials, discussion topics are handed out in the beginning and you have time to think of how to respond. Time for exams is quite short, though the number of questions on the midterm and final is also low.
sections.workload: Not too heavy, open-book exam so important to review slides to know where to find information, but readings on reserve in library are optional but very useful to understanding course modules.

sections.content: It talks about Contemporary China, which was the period after 1949. The things are very easy to understand and follow if you have very basic knowledge about China or have studied liberal studies about modern china in high school. It does not really matter whether you have studied history in high school or not because the professor explains things in a very detailed way that even me who have no history background can understand all the stuff.
sections.teaching: I would say the professor is one of my favorite professors in UST. You can feel his passion in teaching that he is well-prepared. He can speak very fluently and with good pronunciation despite the fact that he comes from the mainland.  The only thing that may not be very good to most students is that his tone is so flat that many may easily fall asleep.
sections.grading: It is really good when comparing the workload and the final results. To be honest, listen to what he said in the lessons and have a quick look at the lecture notes just before the exam is good enough already. The exam questions are not very tricky and most importantly is an open book one! There are 25 questions in mid-term which last for one hour and 40 questions in the final exam which last for 2 hours. You can easily get a B range in this course, which may be better than those courses that the average score is around C+.
sections.workload: 0 workload, just need to revise before the mid-term and final exam. Really good!

sections.content: The content is mainly about the history,culture after the PRC rules China. I think it is easy to handle.
sections.teaching: Prof. is very nice as he was always willing to answer students' questions. However, I think it is a bit boring.
sections.grading: I think it is quite good, I didn't listen much to his lectures, but only rely on the notes and I finally got a B.
sections.workload: Light workload, only mid term and final, and both open book. However, you should attend every lectures as attendance is counted.

sections.content: The content of the class is very interesting. I learned a lot through this course and the professor seems very passionate about the materials covered in the class.
sections.teaching: The pace can be too quick at first but once the student adapts and discovers an efficient way to take notes during the lectures, exams become easier as the tests are open-note.
sections.grading: It depends on how well the student takes notes during lectures and how focused he/she is during class.
sections.workload: No out of work assignment but it is recommended to review your notes often.

sections.teaching: It's boring. The professor basically reads out what was on the ppt.
sections.grading: Grading is really good. I got an A- even though I skipped almost 5 classes. For mid-term, out of 25 questions I got 23. And for final exam, I got 35 out of 40. I didn't even go to class or study because it's an open book exam.
sections.workload: Attendance is 10%. But other than that there are only two open book exams. You will also gain extra points if you ask or answer questions during lectures or tutorials. You also do not have to do any readings.

sections.content: major developments and changes in China since 1949 from a multidisciplinary social science perspective. Topics include the background and structure of the State and the Government, Socialist Economy and Economic Reform, Rural-Urban Divide, The Work Unit System etc. For those who takes DSE has learnt some concepts in the subject of liberal studies.
sections.teaching: Each lecture lasts for 1 hour and 50 minutes, one lecture each week. The teaching is quite boring, just go through the PPT with 90% words and 10% graphic stuffs. You don't need to participate actively in class as no participating cards are given but there are some pop-quiz in random lectures which take attendance, and your correct answers are counted in this area. Tutorial classes are even more interesting than the lectures where videos or documentary films of modern of China is played and it lasts for almost a hour. After that, there are some discussions on that videos, just easy stuffs, and attendance is counted in tutorials.
sections.grading:
I have scored above mean 0.5 sd in both the mid-term examination as well as the final examination which gives me B+ finally.

Course assessment :
Participation 15%
Mid-term exam 35%
Final exam 35%
Term paper 15%
sections.workload: Best part of the project in this course is individual essay which accounts for 15%. You may choose any topics learnt in lectures and to discover it deeply. For mid term and final examination, it is all bout memorizing the PPT, most of the questions come from the PPT. I don't recommend you just studying all the things in the study break, it will be hard to memorize all stuffs. It is reminded that it is a closed-book examination, while the lecture for another professor is opened-book examination.

If you want to have good grades in this course, study hard.
